To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) meta-learning is not the solution for few-shot classification, (2) the performance of few-shot classification is not correlated to the number of training examples, (3) the performance of meta-learning models is not correlated to their ability to learn from multiple datasets.

(1) the current state of the art in few-shot learning is still very far from human-level performance; (2) there is a large gap between the best performance on the most common few-shot learning benchmarks and the best performance on Meta-Dataset; (3) there are many ways to improve the performance on few-shot learning benchmarks, but these ways are not necessarily helpful for improving the performance on Meta-Datasets.

(1) we introduce Meta-Dataset, a large-scale, diverse, and realistic dataset for evaluating meta-learning models, (2) we propose a novel method that achieves state-of-the-art results on Meta-Dataset and other few-shot classification benchmarks, and (3) we provide an extensive analysis of the models’ performance and their ability to leverage diverse datasets for improving generalization.
In summary, our research is concerned with
improving the evaluation and training of models in few-shot learning and our proposed benchmark, Meta-Dataset, aims to be a step in that direction.
improving the state of the art in few-shot classification by proposing Meta-Dataset as a benchmark, a new method, and new baselines.

the following: (1) How can we better evaluate and compare models that learn from few examples?, (2) Can models that learn from diverse sources generalize well in few-shot learning?, and (3) How can we improve the state-of-the-art in few-shot learning?

Meta-Dataset provides a new benchmark for few-shot learning that is both large-scale and diverse and that can be used to assess the progress of new methods in a principled way.
we are far from solving few-shot learning.
we have a new benchmark for learning to learn from few examples that is large-scale and diverse and presents more realistic few-shot classification tasks.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the best performing model in our experiments is the one that uses the most training data.
we present a new dataset and a set of new baselines that can be used to better evaluate the progress of models for few-shot classification.
the performance of current meta-learned models is still far from ideal and that we need to improve the training and evaluation protocols to better understand their strengths and limitations.

we need to develop new methods for learning to learn from few examples that are more robust to the diversity and scale of real-world tasks.
we should move away from the current practice of using small-scale datasets to evaluate few-shot classification methods.
